summary: Lists requirements for reliable server pooling, where a group of servers can back each other up and clients can reach a working one. It is the requirements groundwork for protocols of that kind. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3237 lists what a group of cooperating servers needs to do. It explains how servers join or leave the group, how clients find an available server, and how the system responds to failures.

subtitle: Requirements for pooling servers so clients can reach an available service.

tldr.problem: Applications may need a service to remain available when a server fails. RFC 3237 records requirements for an architecture that manages groups of servers and lets clients reach them.
tldr.mechanism: It requires support for failure detection, alternate servers, server registration and removal, name resolution, and different server-selection policies.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC sets requirements for future Reliable Server Pooling architecture and protocols; it does not specify those protocols.

today: RFC 3237 is an Informational requirements document. The RFC describes goals for a future RSerPool architecture and protocols, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Purpose and Pooling Terms
sections.content:
RFC 3237 sets requirements for Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool), an architecture intended to manage server pools and let clients access them. A pool is a group of servers that provide the same application function. A pool handle is the logical name used to identify that group within an operation scope.

An individual registered server is a pool element, and a client using the service is a pool user. A name server manages the namespace that records pool names and relationships. The RFC defines these roles but does not specify a protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes a group of servers that offer the same service. It defines the names for the group, its servers, its users, and the service that keeps track of them.

sections.title: Failure Handling and Network Use
sections.content:
The architecture must avoid a single point of failure. It must detect failures of pool elements and name servers, then support switching to available alternatives. It should also permit different communication arrangements between clients and servers, including peer-to-peer use.

Pool-management protocols should avoid heavy network traffic, including during failures, and must use flow control and congestion avoidance compatible with TCP and SCTP practices. The architecture should not depend on multicast, though it may use multicast when available. It should also support devices with different processing capacities and conceal network failures from applications as much as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server or the service that tracks the group fails, the system must be able to detect the failure and use another resource. Its management messages must not overload the network, and it should work on devices with different capabilities.

sections.title: Registration, Names and Server Selection
sections.content:
Servers should be able to register with a pool or leave it without interrupting service for clients already connected to them. After a server leaves, new connections should go to another pool element. A server may belong to multiple pools, and pool handles are valid only within their operation scope.

Name resolution should not return a pool element that is not operational. The system must support multiple server-selection policies, such as Round Robin, Least Used and Most Used, and allow policies to be extended. Clients should be able to report operational status, and some applications need a way to reconnect to the same server while it remains available.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can stop accepting new clients while continuing to serve existing ones. The system should direct new clients to an available server using a selected rule.

sections.title: Timing, Scale and Security
sections.content:
Name lookups should be fast enough for real-time applications, and clients should learn about pool changes without waiting for their next connection. The RFC limits its timing goals to pools of a suitably large but not Internet-wide size. It expects the name servers for a pool to form a flat set of equivalent servers, rather than requiring a hierarchy.

The security requirements include preventing false pool-element registrations, unauthorized deregistration, and forged name-server responses. The system should protect the privacy of queries and replies and protect communication among name servers. Sharing or transferring application security state during failover is outside the scope of RSerPool and must be addressed by applications or future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should learn about pool changes quickly, while the system stays within a size that supports timely lookups. It must also stop outsiders from faking server records or changing a pool without permission.
